claim: Dcc is a transmembrane receptor discovered as a potential tumor suppressor.
source: Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (Dcc) is a transmembrane receptor discovered as a potential tumor suppressor (Pierceall et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierceall et al., 1994

claim: Dcc binds the extracellular matrix protein Netrin-1.
source: Dcc binds the extracellular matrix protein Netrin-1 (Keino-Masu et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keino-Masu et al., 1996 and Serafini et al., 1994

claim: When bound to Netrin-1, Dcc activates downstream signaling partners such as MAP kinase, focal adhesion kinase (FAK) or Src kinases which ultimately influence cytoskeleton dynamics and cell motility.
source: When bound to Netrin-1, Dcc activates downstream signaling partners such as MAP kinase, focal adhesion kinase (FAK) or Src kinases which ultimately influence cytoskeleton dynamics and cell motility (Mehlen et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mehlen et al., 2011 and Ren et al., 2004

claim: Dcc is a dependence receptor which triggers cell death in absence of Netrin-1.
source: However, Dcc is also a dependence receptor (Mehlen et al., 2011; Mehlen et al., 1998) which triggers cell death in absence of Netrin-1 (Llambi et al., 2005; Mehlen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mehlen et al., 2011; Mehlen et al., 1998; Llambi et al., 2005

claim: Direct evidence linking Dcc to tumorigenesis was obtained in mice.
source: Although direct evidence linking Dcc to tumorigenesis was obtained in mice (Castets et al., 2012; Krimpenfort et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Castets et al., 2012 and Krimpenfort et al., 2012

claim: Mutations in DCC were identified in patients suffering from congenital mirror movements.
source: mutations in DCC were also identified in patients suffering from rare neurodevelopmental disorders including congenital mirror movements (Depienne et al., 2011; Srour et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Depienne et al., 2011 and Srour et al., 2010

claim: Mutations in DCC were identified in patients suffering from corpus callosum dysgenesis.
source: mutations in DCC were also identified in patients suffering from rare neurodevelopmental disorders including congenital mirror movements (Depienne et al., 2011; Srour et al., 2010) and corpus callosum dysgenesis (Jamuar et al., 2017; Marsh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jamuar et al., 2017 and Marsh et al., 2017

claim: Dcc is present in the developing central nervous system (CNS) and controls axon guidance and cell migration in the spinal cord, as well as in multiple brain areas.
source: Dcc is present in the developing central nervous system (CNS) and controls axon guidance and cell migration in the spinal cord, as well as in multiple brain areas (Belle et al., 2014; Fazeli et al., 1997; Fothergill et al., 2014; Laumonnerie et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2014; Srivatsa et al., 2014; Yee et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Belle et al., 2014; Fazeli et al., 1997; Fothergill et al., 2014; Laumonnerie et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2014; Srivatsa et al., 2014; Yee et al., 1999

claim: Dcc expression persists in the postnatal and adult CNS where it is involved in synaptogenesis.
source: Dcc expression persists in the postnatal and adult CNS where it is involved in synaptogenesis (Horn et al., 2013; Manitt et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Horn et al., 2013 and Manitt et al., 2013

claim: Dcc is involved in myelination in the postnatal and adult CNS.
source: Dcc expression persists in the postnatal and adult CNS where it is involved in synaptogenesis (Horn et al., 2013; Manitt et al., 2013) and myelination (Jarjour et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jarjour et al., 2008

claim: Dcc knockout (KO) mice lack Dcc in all cells.
source: In vivo evidence supporting Dcc function in CNS development was primarily obtained using Dcc knockout (KO) mice (a null allele) which lack Dcc in all cells (Fazeli et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fazeli et al., 1997

claim: A hypoplasia of the optic nerve was reported in the visual system of Dcc KO mice.
source: One of the most striking phenotype, a hypoplasia of the optic nerve, was reported in the visual system (Deiner et al., 1997; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deiner et al., 1997 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: In Dcc KO embryos, a large fraction of the retinal ganglion cell (RGC) axons is unable to exit the retina.
source: In Dcc KO embryos, a large fraction of the retinal ganglion cell (RGC) axons which connects the eye to the brain via the optic nerve is unable to exit the retina (Deiner et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deiner et al., 1997

claim: Netrin-1 is present at the optic disc, the exit point of the retina.
source: The presence of its ligand Netrin-1 at the optic disc, the exit point of the retina, together with the presence of hypoplasic optic nerves in Ntn1 hypomorph mutant embryos suggested that Netrin-1 acts as a long range cue attracting Dcc-expressing RGC axons towards the optic nerve head (Deiner et al., 1997; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deiner et al., 1997 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: Ntn1 hypomorph mutant embryos have hypoplasic optic nerves.
source: The presence of its ligand Netrin-1 at the optic disc, the exit point of the retina, together with the presence of hypoplasic optic nerves in Ntn1 hypomorph mutant embryos suggested that Netrin-1 acts as a long range cue attracting Dcc-expressing RGC axons towards the optic nerve head (Deiner et al., 1997; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deiner et al., 1997 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: Netrin-1 was suggested to act as a long range cue attracting Dcc-expressing RGC axons towards the optic nerve head.
source: The presence of its ligand Netrin-1 at the optic disc, the exit point of the retina, together with the presence of hypoplasic optic nerves in Ntn1 hypomorph mutant embryos suggested that Netrin-1 acts as a long range cue attracting Dcc-expressing RGC axons towards the optic nerve head (Deiner et al., 1997; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deiner et al., 1997 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: Dcc expression persists in RGC axons after they exit the retina and even postnatally.
source: Dcc expression persists in RGC axons after they exit the retina and even postnatally (Shi et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi et al., 2010

claim: Dcc null mice die at birth.
source: but as Dcc null mice die at birth (Fazeli et al., 1997), its function at later stages of visual system development is unknown.

claim: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, Netrin-1 attracts RGC axons toward the optic disc.
source: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, Netrin-1 attracts RGC axons toward the optic disc (Shewan et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Shewan et al., 2002

claim: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, Netrin-1 promotes RGC axon arborization and synapse formation within the tectum.

evidence: Supported by citation to Manitt et al., 2009

claim: Recent studies using conditional knockout strategies have suggested that Netrin-1 does not act as a long-range attractive cue for axons at the CNS midline.
source: Importantly, recent studies using conditional knockout strategies have revisited the role of Netrin-1 in axon guidance at the CNS midline and suggested that Netrin-1 does not act as a long-range attractive cue for axons (Dominici et al., 2017; Moreno-Bravo et al., 2019; Varadarajan et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).

claim: The conditional ablation of Dcc in specific neuronal classes recapitulates the axon guidance defects found in Dcc KO embryos in some systems.

evidence: Supported by citations to da Silva et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2018; Zelina et al., 2014

claim: There is evidence for a non-cell autonomous role of Dcc in cortical projection neurons.
source: there is also evidence for a non-cell autonomous role in cortical projection neurons (Welniarz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Welniarz et al., 2017

claim: Eye-specific Dcc mutants are fully viable.

evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: At E11, Dcc-immunoreactive cells co-localized with the early RGC marker, Islet1.

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B and citation to Austin et al., 1995
